item.title: Replacing Female Stereotypes With Empowering Archetypes
item.description:
Bias

Replacing Female Stereotypes With Empowering Archetypes

Which deeply entrenched stereotypes about women might you hold unconsciously?

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Gender bias rewards assertiveness in male leaders but can penalize the same trait in women.
  • Judgments of women’s likability and appearance can overshadow their policies and competence.
  • Rosalind Cardinal identifies four positive leadership archetypes a woman can embody.
“We Can Do It!” (1943) poster by J. Howard Miller (1898-1985)
Source: National Archives at College Park / Public Domain

As humans, we all have unconscious biases that influence our most important choices: where we live and with whom; who we consider friends and enemies; who we choose to govern; what we believe about our universe and about God. It may be impossible to rid ourselves of all our biases, but we can become aware of them and how they shape our decisions. Biases lead us to create stereotypes of people or ideas, and these stereotypes can limit our interactions with and understanding of others and the world.

With early voting, many Americans have already gone to the polls or will go in less than a week. What leadership qualities do you consider essential in a candidate? Does a candidate’s gender affect your evaluation? Do you consider some personality traits as masculine or feminine? Take a minute to remember when and how you first developed these beliefs.

In 1984, psychiatrist and Jungian analyst Jean Shibola Bolen wrote a revolutionary book, Goddesses in Everywoman: A New Psychology of Women. Bolen’s aim was to deter women from identifying with repressive cultural stereotypes that narrowed their self-image, capabilities, and role in society. Using the Greek goddesses as models, Bolen offered modern women portraits of the female deities that represented archetypal patterns still active in modern women’s psyches.

Women might discover their “inner Athena,” the warrior goddess, ally to male heroes and known for her strategic prowess in battle. Born fully formed from her father Zeus’s head, Athena was depicted in full battle armor—breastplate, helmet, spear—and honored for her practical intelligence and sound planning. Bolen examined seven goddess types—nurturing Demeter, intuitive Persephone, calm Hestia, queenly Hera, creative Aphrodite, and autonomous Artemis—each with her own backstory and attributes, breaking through old stereotypes and providing exciting examples for a more expansive self. The book was an instant best-seller and changed how many women viewed themselves.1

It’s been 40 years since the publication of Goddesses in Everywoman. Yet our country is one of the few Western democracies that has not yet elected a female president. But change may be coming. According to the Center for American Women and Politics (CAWP), a record number of 4,215 women are running for nationwide or state office in 2026: 271 for seats in the House of Representatives, 19 for Senate seats, 131 for statewide executive offices, including governor, and 3,794 for state legislatures.2 It’s a good time to examine our stereotypical biases about leaders and leadership.

Women seeking leadership positions, across cultures and throughout time, face challenges their male cohorts do not. Rather than being evaluated for their policies and ideology, women are judged on the basis of likability and presentation. A woman candidate can be seen as too assertive, or conversely, too empathetic and too weak to lead. Aggressiveness, a trait valued in a male candidate (he’ll get things done for us, he’ll stop the war, vanquish the enemy), is seen as a negative trait in a female candidate. A female candidate must strike just the right balance between not being too masculine and lacking empathy, or too feminine and lacking the moxie and stamina to be a leader.

Women candidates are judged by their wardrobe, hair, makeup, weight, body size, their beauty or lack of it, tone of voice and gestural language, and a host of other factors that do not include intelligence and competency. Shared cultural stereotypes exist in most societies, and women and marginalized groups are more vulnerable to prejudices that don’t align with accepted norms.3

Some of the most accepted stereotypes women face include:

  • Women are natural nurturers; men are natural leaders
  • Women with children are less devoted to their jobs
  • Women are too emotional to undertake certain kinds of work, especially while pregnant
  • Assertive women are “bossy, bitches, or whores”4

Rosalind Cardinal, a facilitator, leadership coach, and speaker, spent years researching the different ways men and women lead. She was especially interested in learning how women uniquely approach leadership roles. Writing from her experience in human resources and as a leadership mentor, she saw a need to expand the repertoire of archetypal models for future female leaders. Since 2018, over 10,000 women have participated in her Women Leader Archetypes (WLA) assessment. Drawing on findings from this expansive dataset, she devised four basic patterns of female leadership. In practice, one individual can exhibit all four of these characteristics.

The Sovereign

“Self-assured, focused on being her best, fearless leader, confident, exciting, influential, impactful, magnetic, uses her power to benefit the collective, creative. Sovereign thinking results in the highest form of personal fulfilment. This archetype is characterized by a very high acceptance of self, others, and situations “as they are." Sovereign women feel in control of their lives and have achieved a unique sense of self-acceptance, self-respect, and pride in what they do.”

The Warrior

“Ambitious, change catalyst, goal-driven, visionary, insightful problem solver, loves challenges, a true self-starter, motivated, sure of her ability. The Warrior archetype is highly associated with personal effectiveness. Warriors are focused, goal-oriented individuals who are proficient at attaining high-quality results on challenging projects. Warriors are motivated to succeed by their own values and beliefs. They know they can improve things and do not hesitate to act on this knowledge.”

The Wise Woman

“Sought out by others for her wisdom and knowledge, she is a lifelong learner who mentors, guides, and encourages others. Shares her knowledge freely. Supports the growth of others, sees potential. Wise Women believe they can assist others in fulfilling their potential by providing a supportive environment that inspires self-improvement. They gain satisfaction from seeing others learning and growing, and their willingness to take time with people makes them excellent leaders and coaches. They are very knowledgeable and sought out by others for their words of wisdom.”

The Tribe Builder

“Networker draws people together, creates community and collectiveness, compassionate, empathic, values people and relationships. The Tribe Builder archetype tends to value relationships and connections above all else. She has a need to build relationships that are meaningful, and she possesses strong, well-developed interpersonal skills. The Tribe Builder motivates primarily with genuine praise and friendliness.”5

Cardinal’s typology is an invitation to ponder what traits and values we want in our leaders. It’s also an invitation to root out stereotypical thinking about those we consider Other. Animals of different species often find comfort in each other and become lifelong friends. After watching a video of the devoted friendship between Owen, an orphaned hippo in Kenya, and his dear buddy Mzee, a 130-year-old giant tortoise,6 or seeing Ruuxa, a rejected cheetah cub at the San Diego Zoo, comforted by a puppy named Raina,7 you might feel your own fear of unfamiliar others loosen its grip.

item.title: The Effect of Body Shaming on the Ability to Feel Pleasure
item.description:
Body Image

The Effect of Body Shaming on the Ability to Feel Pleasure

Body shaming is implicated in an inability to experience pleasure, even desire.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Anhedonia—the inability to experience pleasure, even desire and joy—is often a result of body shaming.
  • Body shaming didn’t start with social media or dieting fads; it began in primitive times as social comparison.
  • Catching oneself in the act of self-shaming helps counter the long-standing effects of body shaming.
Source: Pixabay/Alex_Bon_Space

A friend of mine who was raised in a very Catholic family once told me that her mother used to refer to her vagina as her “icky,” as in, “Now wipe your icky.” This makes it not the least bit surprising that, as an adult, she thinks of her vagina as unattractive. “A weird little organ,” she calls it. “I can’t put makeup on it.”

It’s also not surprising that Sigmund Freud would observe that “the suppression of a woman’s sexuality”—in this case by a mother’s inadvertent body shaming—“leads to a general inhibition of desire and curiosity, a restriction on wanting and knowing that spreads throughout her life.”

Body shaming—criticizing or demeaning someone’s appearance, overtly or covertly—is linked to what psychologists call dysmorphia, an unhealthy preoccupation with your body’s perceived flaws, which tends to generalize to your perception of yourself. In relationships, it often shows up as a lack of intimacy, because you don’t want anyone getting close enough to see those flaws.

Body shaming is also implicated in something called anhedonia, the inability to experience pleasure, since pleasure begins with the body and its senses.

The Origins of Body Shaming

Contrary to popular belief, body shaming didn’t start with the rise of social media, or the "Mad Men" era of advertising in the '50s and '60s, or even the dieting and exercise fads of the last 200 years. It began in primitive times as social comparison, the innate human impulse to gauge your personal and social worth in a tribe by how you stack up against others.

It also grew out of ancient superstitions that, for instance, red hair was a sign of bad luck or bad temper, green eyes were marks of the devil, and a slender body type emblematic of poverty—superstitions that turned into prejudices and beauty standards whose bruising effect is very hard to undo.

But what really fused body shaming with anhedonia were puritanical religions and philosophies throughout human history, with their discriminations and damnations against the pleasures of the body; their insistence that the body is something to jettison on your way to the divine; their belief that sexual thoughts are a distracting impurity, a fly in the ointment of virtue; and the promulgation of ideas like original sin, which is stone-cold guaranteed to shame people to the core.

Gnosticism, a theology related to early Christianity and Judaism, referred to the body as “a corpse with senses, the grave you carry around with you.” Both Socrates and Plato in ancient Greece viewed all forms of sexuality as inferior to abstinence because it involved the body. The medieval Pope Gregory declared that “sensual pleasure can never be without sin.” The temptations encountered by Christ in Judea, Buddha under the bodhi tree, and St. Anthony in the Egyptian desert are almost universally depicted in art as either naked women or demons and monsters.

Reframing Sensual and Sexual Pleasure

It’s critical to understand something about these spurious correlations between the body and blasphemy, sensual pleasure and sin, even the erotic and the perverted: The word "perverted" means to be turned from what’s natural and normal. The body’s sensual and sexual capacities are natural and normal to humans, and by definition whatever blocks their energies, whatever turns us against our own bodies, is what’s perverted.

Our bodies were naturally designed for sensual experience and pleasure. We’re endowed with over 1,000 nerve endings per square inch over our entire body, 10,000 taste buds on the tongue, another 10,000 aromas we can discern with our noses, and a heavenly host of appetites toward which to apply these endowments.

On the other hand, we’ve been told that the supposedly intelligent designer of these gifts is disgusted by our use of them. This is strangely and tragically ironic. If we’re indeed made in the image of God, as the Bible says, by rejecting our bodies we’re also rejecting God—in ourselves and in others, those neighbors we’re instructed to love as ourselves.

The Body as a Channel for Spiritual Experience

What all these teachers and teachings have been telling us—confounding us with—for thousands of years is that our bodies, with their natural and God-given passions, are corrupt and corrupting, and in fact work against our spiritual passions. But the body isn’t an obstacle to spirit and soul, a mere skin to shed on the way to some incredible lightness of being. It’s a channel to them.

The famous Bernini sculpture of a swooning St. Theresa in the Santa Maria Della Vittoria church in Rome—an angel about to thrust the arrow of God’s love into her—is a classic example of how indistinguishable spiritual and orgasmic rapture can be. The Song of Solomon and the texts of tantra both use highly erotic language to describe union with the sacred.

Now surely some of our “temptations”—including a compulsive preoccupation with how we look—can and do interfere with our higher aspirations for ourselves, and create real suffering. But they’re also among our greatest earthly pleasures and shouldn’t be thrown out with the mortal bathwater. (Besides, it was a sensual pleasure that gave each of us life.)

“The historical and psychological splitting of spirit and body,” says Thomas Moore in The Soul of Sex, “of transcendence and sensuousness, virtue and desire, is a neurosis. A disturbance of the soul.” And we are its descendants. Not just we as individuals, but we the people. Your relationship with your own body—and the feeling of being at home there—is on the same continuum as your relationship to the body politic and the body of Earth.

How to Counter Self-Shaming and Reclaim Bodily Pleasure

Reclaiming your body and its pleasures requires disclaiming the judgments and prohibitions against them that were passed down by your forebears, and recapitulated by social media, advertising and beauty standards. But undoing the spell and unshaming yourself also require regular intervention, catching yourself in the act of self-shaming and applying a compensating counter-message.

For example, rather than focusing on how your body looks, focus on the voluminous and miraculous things it can do: enjoy the taste of food, the sensation of dancing, the beauty of nature and art, the rapture of music, the tingle of loving touch, the pleasure of being immersed in water, the exaltation of being able to climb mountains and take in a bigger picture.

item.title: Halloween Costumes: Are We Hiding or Expressing Ourselves?
item.description:
Deception

Halloween Costumes: Are We Hiding or Expressing Ourselves?

What is wearing a mask good for?

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Wearing costumes is a natural, fun way to learn about ourselves.
  • Costumes and masks have the power to influence others' ideas about us.
  • When we embrace our true selves underneath our costumes, transformation happens.
Source: Tracy Strauss

When I was five, on Halloween I dressed up as a cat. My mother sewed my costume from felt and painted whiskers on my face using her black liquid eyeliner. I stood happily in our front yard, excited to try on the identity of someone other than myself. When I was eight, my costume preference changed: I was a nurse. At eleven, I was the Queen of Hearts.

Halloween is a time when many of us transform ourselves into an “other” for a day. Go inside any Home Goods or TJ Maxx right now and you’ll find a plethora of costumes and masks.

The word “mask” is rooted in the ancient Latin term, “persona.” In the early 20th century, Carl Jung defined a persona as a social mask, one that makes an impression upon others while masking one’s true self. (A side note on Jung’s doggedness: As a young man, Jung suffered from debilitating mental health issues. His response to his own suicidality was to engage in self-analysis, which led him to transmute his own pain into purpose: he originated the school of psychoanalytic psychology.) Long ago, stage actors wore masks to represent or project the personality of a character.

Making an Impression on Others

In psychology, the term “enclothed cognition” refers to how what we wear influences our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, and how what we wear can also influence how others see us. Wearing a suit, for example, may elicit the idea that we are professional, have high standards, or that we belong to a certain social class. Dressing up as a superhero on Halloween may make us feel empowered, creative, or transcendent, and garner respect from others.

Source: Tracy Strauss

Sometimes we’re required to wear a certain outfit for our occupation. The Amazon uniform, for example, includes a company vest, identifying the wearer as its official representative. Such gear emits the philosophy and values of the organization, which may be in conflict with the wearer’s own sensibilities.

Our chosen costumes and masks create responses—thoughts, beliefs, and emotional reactions—in those around us. My dog, Beau, for example, considers everyone who wears a USPS, UPS, or FedEx uniform as safe, good people. He will seek them out on the street, in a building lobby, or in their vehicles, smiling and wagging his tail. However, show him someone dressed as the Grim Reaper, or a drug dealer, and he will bark and lunge and show his teeth.

Deceiving Others

At its worst, masks can trick or deceive: a wolf in sheep’s clothing. In The Wizard of Oz, the "great and almighty" Oz isn’t really “great and almighty,” but small, petty, and weak.

A few years ago, when Beau was attending doggie daycare, on Halloween they had a bobbing for biscuits party with a costume contest. The manager asked me if Beau would be willing to dress up as Sharkboy so that she could be his Lavagirl. She called Beau the daycare’s “best behaved dog.” Beau was not into wearing a costume but he donned some shark fins (which I provided) for a few seconds, looking at the daycare's camera with what appeared to be ghastliness. Not long after, the manager began drinking on the job and her negligence resulted in a problem dog viciously attacking Beau, causing severe injury. The manager dismissed Beau from daycare and allowed the offending dog to stay. Beau and the manager's projected Sharkboy-Lavagirl bond had been for appearances only. In reality, it was nothing but a sham.

Concealing or Showcasing Ourselves

Do all masks deceive or conceal our authentic selves? It depends on the wearer. As a five-year-old, I wasn’t a feline species, but my cat costume was an expression of my true self: playful, loving, curious, and at times feisty and defiant.

One study, “Playing Dress-Up: Costumes, Role Play, and Imagination,” found that in wearing costumes, we learn more about ourselves.

Source: Tracy Strauss

Beau’s preferred costume wear is a lion's mane. For Halloween, two years in a row, he dressed as the cowardly lion from The Wizard of Oz; although he had an anxiety disorder, as he recovered from the daycare assault, he learned that he had more courage than he ever knew.

Today, Beau prefers to go as himself: a dog. As a dog, his true self is unencumbered by any costume. He doesn't tolerate masks. He expresses himself in uncensored ways, in any situation.

Over our years together, Beau’s doggedness—of species and of spirit—and has taught me a lot about persisting, unapologetically, as our true selves.

This Halloween, if you find yourself donning a mask or a full costume, take a moment to notice what that mask or costume expresses about your underlying wishes, values, or even your pain. Remember that, at the end of the day, there’s nothing and nowhere to hide. When you remove the mask and doggedly embrace your genuine self, that’s when true transformation, and happiness, happen.

item.title: What's Your Passion? Where Has It Gone?
item.description:
Career

What's Your Passion? Where Has It Gone?

3 steps to reignite your life.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • As we move through our lives, our sense of passion often withers, replaced by routines and habits,
  • But passion can fuel our lives, drive a sense of purpose. The key is to step and take stock of our lives.
  • By acting on small burst of excitement or preference, and experimenting we can reignite our passion.
Source: Pexels/pixabay

Our own lives naturally wither: physically, as our bodies gradually deteriorate, and often psychologically as well. Where once you were driven by the desire to raise kids or climb the corporate ladder, and where once you threw yourself into creative outlets—music, writing, art—you’re now driven by habit, routines, and the demands of simply keeping your life moving forward. Passion that once fueled your life has now withered, pushed to the back burner for good reasons. And if your life has changed—the kids are gone, you’ve settled on some corporate rung, you’re facing retirement and are unclear about your sense of purpose—the need to bring passion back into your life is all the stronger and more important. Passion can fuel change.

The challenge is to bring it back, to stop running on autopilot or accepting what you’ve got. The accumulation of such a life often reaches its tipping point in midlife, when you sense time is running out and your life is narrowing, prompting many to quit their careers or get divorced to bring energy and passion back into their lives.

But you don’t need to wait for a crisis to reignite your life. Here are three steps to help you rediscover and re-energize yourself:

#1: Step back:

Start here. Take stock. As you survey the vast landscape of your life, ask what’s missing. If you were to build your life from scratch, what would be different? What from your past do you need to reclaim—your interest in music or art, your belief in yourself, or your spontaneity? Try to avoid getting caught up in generalities—more money, ideally a different partner—and instead go one level deeper to focus on what they may represent—less anxiety, more common interests, more excitement. These are stepping stones toward where you want to go and who you want to become.

#2: Act on the smallest spark.

Rediscovering your passion can feel like a big challenge, especially if you’ve neglected those feelings for so long. You can start smaller by focusing on what you prefer. This is about rewiring your brain by noticing and acting on anything outside your routine that gives you a slight jolt of novelty. This is the baby step toward cultivating passion.

And if you feel passionate about something—to get back into music or art, study birds, or shake up your relationship or work—resist your critical brain's urge to sweep it under the rug because it deems it impractical or stupid. Act, but not impulsively—don’t quit your job. Wait until your rational brain is back online, gather information, and plan next steps. Use your emotions as information, not as jet fuel.

#3: Experiment.

Some of the sparks may peter out—you may find that your old or new interests no longer hold your attention. No loss, because you’ve learned something; life is a process of elimination. Adopt an attitude of curiosity rather than revolution, and of experimentation rather than makeovers.

All this reminds me of a Wendell Berry quote: When you don’t know what to do, you’ve found your real work, and when you don’t know where to go, you’ve begun your journey.

Do the work and enjoy the journey.

item.title: What Years of Pop Lyrics Tell Leaders About the Room
item.description:
Leadership

What Years of Pop Lyrics Tell Leaders About the Room

Every leader is walking into a room shaped by decades of cultural drift.

Posted October 30, 2026

If you’ve ever had the thought that the world seems crankier now than it was when you were 12, or that something about the post- pandemic world seems more chaotic and darker than it did before—well, researchers have turned up some data that suggests it’s even worse than you think.

The researchers in question analyzed the last 60 years of pop song lyrics – something like 400,000 songs– to track the worldview indicated by the language in them. And the results are disturbing: we’re singing about cheating, harm, degradation, anger, and disgust way more often, and decency, care, and other virtues way less (Preniqi et al., Scientific Reports, 2026).

I’m sorry to report, gentlemen, that male pop singers are more likely to embrace the dark side than women. The point is that pop music reflects society, how it feels about itself and what it thinks about the world, and that visage in the mirror has been getting nastier and nastier over the 60 years tested.

Other researchers have confirmed these sad findings in various ways. The top hits have become more about negative emotions. Pop music has become more about “me” than anyone else. Words like “serenity” and “joy” are gradually disappearing, to be replaced by their negative counterparts.

What pop tunes tell us probably matters not just because of how it reflects social trends, but also in how it shapes them. A pop hit can become an anthem and teach millions of impressionable kids how to give voice to their emotions – and pull them toward the dark side by making it OK to identify with those feelings.

A few years ago, in 2021, I wrote about the 20th anniversary of 9/11 and found myself thinking along similar lines. Reflecting on how the communications world had changed, I noted five trends: gatekeepers giving way to do-it-yourself social media, a thirst for more authentic voices, executives having to become vulnerable storytellers, some progress on inclusivity, and mostly, speed. As we’ve all experienced, the world keeps hurtling faster toward the future, every moment. Mostly, and tragically, the world forever lost some of its joy on 9/11. This 60-year study of pop tunes suggests that it hasn’t been a blip caused by a world-shaking event, but rather a gradual, and measurable, slide into the dark.

Let’s take a moment to mourn the loss of joy in the world. We’re no longer capable of the innocent joys that once made our eyes light up. Similarly, the mechanized slaughter of WWI killed a generation’s ideas about honor and chivalry in war – for better and for worse, but mostly for worse.

If we pull in other suggestive research about the hybrid world – HBR’s study about how hybrid workplaces have weaker cultural connections – and the alarming finding that Americans are scoring lower on IQ tests across the board – and we have reason to be alarmed about the state of so-called Western Civ. Put these things together and
they paint an alarming picture of our state of mind here in the U.S. and Europe.

What can leaders do about this? Should they preach to the choir, and talk more doom and gloom? I don’t think that’s the answer, and I don’t think it’s helpful to ignore these trends either. I think that rather leaders need to reflect honestly what they are seeing and still hold out a vision of a more positive future that we might all work toward.

Let’s step up to the difficult moment we find ourselves in, and point to solutions that give us something beneficial to work toward. This is not the darkest era humanity has ever faced, nor is it a simple matter of hoping for the best. We need leaders who fully embrace both what’s in front of us and what the hard work is we need to undertake
collectively to make it better.

item.title: The Folder She Never Opened
item.description:
Family Dynamics

The Folder She Never Opened

Why belonging and agency work best as partners.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Belonging and agency are two essential human needs that work best as partners.
  • In a win-lose world, belonging can harden into compliance, and agency can go rogue.
  • Relationships built on mutuality make it safer to belong and to still speak up.

Maren brought a blue folder to the shareholder meeting and never opened it.

Inside were eleven pages Maren had spent most of the spring writing: a plan to take the family’s distribution business into a market her father had dismissed twice. She knew the numbers and was clear on the opportunity. She had walked the plan past two outside advisors, who deliberately poked holes in it before they confirmed it was sound. She set the folder on the table next to her coffee, listened to her brother go through the quarterly results, laughed at her uncle’s joke about the weather, and drove home with the folder on the passenger seat.

When she told me about it weeks later, she said she felt like an outcast. She had spent the meeting silently worrying that her family would shun her for what they’d see as a challenge to loyalty. Meanwhile everyone carried on with no idea what she was thinking and treated her as completely included. That was what confused her.

I’ve thought about her dilemma ever since. Maren described something I see in my practice all the time, especially with people in family businesses. Acceptance from the people who matter to us does not guarantee the freedom to be ourselves with them.

Beyond survival, we need two things from the people around us. One is belonging: being accepted, valued, and protected by a group. The other is agency: the freedom to express ourselves, affect change, and pursue a purpose that is uniquely our own. Each needs the other. A person who belongs but has no agency gradually loses track of who she is, and independence with no one to belong to has a way of turning rudderless.

The rules of society are mostly organized around winning and losing, which puts these two needs in competition. We learn to belong by accommodating and deferring, and we learn that asserting ourselves puts at risk the safety we draw from our relationships. Speak up, and we may jeopardize our place; stay quiet long enough, and we lose our voice. Under that pressure, belonging hardens into compliance, and agency becomes another way of being alone. Psychologist Vicki Helgeson calls these extremes unmitigated communion and unmitigated agency, and her research links both to poorer health.

Maren knew why she had kept the folder closed. She had watched what happened to her aunt, who pushed for a seat on the board in the nineties, got one, and has not been invited to Thanksgiving since. The lesson in her family was clear enough: a voice or the family, not both. Pick one.

When people talk about balance, they usually mean scheduling: work and family, obligations and personal time, perhaps a workout class squeezed into a Tuesday. Maren’s problem was relational. Can we stay connected to the people we love without surrendering the parts of ourselves that need room to develop?

This is why feeling like an outcast can be so confusing. Sometimes we really have been pushed out by other people. Sometimes we are welcomed everywhere and still feel unseen, because we have learned to hide too much of ourselves. Maren’s aunt was pushed out; Maren kept her seat by keeping the folder closed. Their circumstances look different. Both paid for a family system with no room for individual expression.

In my experience, women are typically taught that belonging comes first and agency has to be earned. Men are taught the reverse: achieve, and belonging will follow. Both messages create problems. Either way, connection and self-expression end up feeling like a trade-off.

So what would it take for Maren to open the blue folder at the family meeting?

She had already done the hard part. The plan had been tested, and it held. What she needed was to think differently about what the folder actually represented.

In her family’s way of thinking, the plan was a sign she was vying for independence, a step away from the table. But for her, the eleven pages were a vote of confidence and a demonstration of care for a business she wants to see thrive. The market her father dismissed twice is a future she was offering them all to see with her. That’s belonging too, even though it risks some friction.

This is the shift I work toward with families. Agency stops competing with belonging when the family learns that what one person develops is something that everyone gains. Families that get there keep their people and get the best from them. The alternative is worth avoiding...pleasant shareholder meetings and an empty chair at Thanksgiving where her aunt should be.

Family enterprises can learn how to stay connected when things get tense, and how to say hard things without letting the relationship go. That’s the emotional capacity it takes to bring a new idea into a family without breaking anything.

In time, Maren saw her plan differently. Rather than a threat to her place in the family, she knew that challenging the system to be better was an act of care that earned her belonging...more than her silence ever had. Maren trusted her intuition, found the words, and developed a new logic. It’s how she’s held her place all these years.
